newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines sees weaker peso helping trade balance.
newsitem.headline: Philippines sees weaker peso helping trade balance.

text.p: The Philippines is likely to attain a trade balance earlier than its target of the year 2001 due to the sharp depreciation of its local currency against the U.S. dollar, Trade Secretary Cesar Bautista said on Monday.
"With this situation, we think this (trade balance) can be advanced," Bautista told a news briefing.
On Friday, the Philippine central bank effectively devalued the peso by allowing it to trade in a wider range.
Analysts have projected a $14 to $16 billion trade deficit this year as new companies set up shop in the country and import equipment for their operations.
The peso fell to a 45-month low of 29.750 early on Monday amid cautious trading, down from Thursday's close of 26.40. Trading was suspended on Friday.
Bautista said the weaker peso could boost export earnings which have been growing by 14 to 16 percent in the first four months of the year, outpacing import bills which have increased 11 percent.
The government is projecting a 20 percent growth in the export sectors this year.

Aside from the present leading exports, such as electronic and computer goods, earnings from traditional exports such as processed agriculture products, furniture and garments were expected to increase after the peso's fall.

"There will be winners, and there'll be very good winners," Philippine Exporters Confederation (Philexport) president Sergio Ortiz-Luis told Reuters. Philexport is the biggest export group in the country.
Ortiz-Luis said he expected the peso to eventually settle five to six percent below Thursday's close of 26.40. He said an exchange rate at that level would not hurt import-dependent exporters.
Electronic and computer-related exports draw heavily from imported components. It is estimated that their products have a 70 to 80 percent import content.
Officials said a robust export sector would be complemented by a slower import growth.
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said imports of non-essential items would be discouraged.
A study by the Department of Finance showed imports will decline by about 2.6 percent for every one peso depreciation.
